title: The Castle Still Burning
subtitle: The Legend of Kagemori Jūrō
teaser: Two hundred and seven retainers swore to die with the last lord of House Asaya. The lord was fourteen years old, and he ordered one of them to live.

sections.heading: I. Eleven Thousand Draws
paragraphs: The heir of House Asaya was fourteen years old. He had drawn his sword more than eleven thousand times, and he had never once done it right.

Kagemori Jūrō knew the exact number because the boy counted out loud. Every morning before dawn, under the persimmon tree in the courtyard, Asaya Matsumaru set his feet, laid his hand on the hilt, breathed, drew, and said a number. And every morning his teacher said the same word.
“Again.”
Jūrō had been sword master to House Asaya for twenty years. Matsumaru was the only pupil he had ever chosen, and the only one he could not teach.

Somewhere between deciding and drawing, the boy stopped to think, and the blade felt the pause and caught for an instant on the mouth of the scabbard. Nobody but a sword master would have seen the hitch. A man could die of it.
“You’re asking a question halfway through,” Jūrō told him.
“What question?”
“Whether the thing in front of you deserves it.”
The boy went red, because it was true. He was the kind of boy who carried spiders out of the practice hall in his cupped hands.
“Then don’t draw,” Jūrō said. “That’s allowed. But if you draw, decide first. The cut is finished before your hand moves. The sword is only the last to find out.”

His sister watched from the veranda, eating persimmons she had been told not to pick. Chiyo was seven, and afraid of nothing except being ignored. She had decided that a teacher who knew one word didn’t need a name, so she called him Uncle Again, to his face.
“Uncle Again,” she said once, through a mouthful of persimmon, “will you ever say anything else to him?”
“When he gives me a reason.”
“What will you say?”
Jūrō considered it. He was not a man who said things he didn’t mean. “Good,” he said.
Chiyo looked at him with deep pity. “That’s very small,” she said. “For eleven thousand.”
In the spring, Matsumaru would turn fifteen and take a man’s name. He never did.

sections.heading: II. The Water Gate
paragraphs: The shogun’s army came that autumn, because Lord Asaya would not send his only son to the capital as a hostage.
The castle held for forty days. On the fortieth, an arrow found Lord Asaya on the east wall, and his son became lord of a house with one night left.

That night two hundred and seven retainers knelt in the great hall, pressed their bloody thumbs beside their names on an oath scroll, and swore to follow their lord into death at dawn. Each wrote his name on a strip of paper and tucked it inside his collar, so whoever found his body in the ashes would know whom they had killed. Jūrō signed eighth. His hand didn’t shake.
At midnight, the boy came to find him. He was wearing his father’s armour, which was too big for him, and carrying Chiyo, asleep with her face in his neck.
“Teacher. The old water gate under the north wall. Can a man still swim it?”
“Just.”
“Then you’ll swim it with her. You’ll take her somewhere safe, and you’ll live. That’s an order. It’s my first.” He almost smiled. “It’ll be my last.”
“I signed the scroll.”
“I watched you.”
“They’ll write my name down as the one who ran.”
“I know. I’m sorry. I thought about that. You told me to decide before my hand moves. I’ve decided.”
Jūrō had watched this boy hesitate eleven thousand times. He looked for the hitch now and couldn’t find it. The cut had been finished before Matsumaru walked into the room.
It was the cleanest draw he had ever seen.

He should have said so. He had one word saved for exactly this. Instead he bowed to the floor and said, “Yes, my lord,” because it was the first time he had ever called the boy that, and his throat would not do anything else.
Jūrō swam the flooded tunnel with Chiyo tied to his back, through water cold enough to stop a heart, and came up in the reeds across the river.
At dawn, the gates of Castle Asaya opened, and two hundred and six men walked out, and a boy in armour too big for him walked first.
By noon, the castle was burning. Chiyo sat in the reeds in Jūrō’s wet coat and watched red sparks drift down onto the river.
“Fireflies,” she said doubtfully. “It’s too cold for fireflies.”
He didn’t tell her.

sections.heading: III. Three Nights
paragraphs: Chiyo had lost a sandal in the tunnel. She cried about that, hard, for the first time since the siege began. Then she stopped, and she didn’t cry again about anything.

He carried her on his shoulders, and she steered him by the ears. The shogun’s men were nailing notices to every village gate: anyone sheltering a survivor of House Asaya would be crucified with their family. One old woman pushed a bowl of cold rice through her shutters, then barred them again, weeping.
On the first evening, by the river, Chiyo stripped a reed and pushed it through her sash like a sword.
“Show me Brother’s thing.”

He showed her. The feet. The breath. The hand resting on the hilt. Decide first. She frowned at the river the way she frowned at a persimmon before she stole it. Then she swept the reed out of her sash in one clean line, with no hitch in it at all.
“Good,” said Jūrō. It was out before he could stop it.
Her whole face lit up. Then it went thoughtful. “Did you ever say that to Brother?”
“No.”
“Not even once?”
“No.”
She held up her smallest finger, very serious. “Then you have to tell him, when we see him. Promise.”
He hooked his finger around hers. It was the second order he had taken from a child of House Asaya in two days. “I promise.”

By the next afternoon she was hot to the touch. The river had got into her chest. He found an empty ferryman’s hut, built a fire, and gave her every bit of warmth he had. It wasn’t enough. Nobody had ever taught him anything for this.
On the third night she woke, and knew him, and wanted to see the sword.
“Do Brother’s thing. Fast.”
He knelt in the dark and drew. She couldn’t have seen the blade. She heard it: the whisper of steel leaving the scabbard, and the small click of the guard coming home.
“Again,” she said.
He drew again. Click.
“Again,” she said, softer.
He drew a third time and slid the blade home. Then he gathered her into his arms and waited for her to say it.
When the sun came up he was still holding her, with one hand on the hilt, ready, in case she asked.

sections.heading: IV. The Register
paragraphs: He buried her under a maple in the yard of a small temple, above a bend in the river. The grave had no name. The shogun had forbidden it.
He cut the gold fittings off his sword and gave them to the old priest, Ensai, with a promise of more every year for as long as he lived.
“Sweep it,” he said. “And talk to her sometimes. She hates being ignored.”

Then he walked back to the castle. The keep had fallen in, and the great cedar beams were still smouldering under the rubble. Outside the ruined gate, the shogun’s clerks were reading out the register of the siege.
Two hundred and six retainers, dead with their lord. Names struck by order. The lord, aged fourteen, dead in the front rank. Name struck by order. The lord’s sister, missing. Name struck by order.
One retainer fled and broke his oath: Kagemori Jūrō, sword master.
That one the clerk wrote out in full. Of all House Asaya, it was the only name the shogun wanted remembered.

That evening he went down to where the water gate let out, and took the strip of paper from his collar. The ink had survived the flood and the fever and the road: his name, in his own hand, written to be found on his body.

He had sworn to die here. He had been ordered to live. A man cannot do both. So he gave the river his name, and let it go where it had been promised. Whatever was left had been ordered to live, and didn’t need a name to do it.
At first light he set his feet on the riverbank and drew the boy’s draw, and the sword came out of the scabbard smoking.
Not steam. Smoke, thick and black and shot with red sparks, smelling of burning cedar. He sheathed and drew again. Smoke.
It has never stopped. Priests have prayed over it; a smith quenched it nine times and gave up. Ask him, and he says only, “It’s the castle. It’s still burning.”

The monks at the temple say a fire promised two hundred and seven men will not go out at two hundred and six. If so, it is still waiting. He was ordered to live, and he has always done what he was told.

sections.heading: V. The Nameless Blade
paragraphs: In the duelling rings they call him the Nameless Blade, because the heralds ask and he won’t say. If they push, he tells them he gave it to the river. He wears a straw hat pulled low, so nobody has to look at the face of the man in the register. His sword has no gold on it.

He fights the way he taught. He stands with his hand on the hilt while his opponents circle and shout, and smoke drifts off him across the ring like the edge of a burning town. Then, once, he draws. If a second cut is needed, it comes straight through his own smoke in a single lunge, trailing embers like sparks off a falling roof.

Young fighters like to announce themselves before a bout: their names, their fathers’ names, their grandfathers’ battles. He listens politely. Then he says, “Your name won’t be remembered. Neither will mine.”

They take it for a threat. It isn’t. He has watched the bravest names he ever knew struck out with one stroke of a clerk’s brush. He means: don’t fight for that. Fight for whatever is still there when the names are gone.

For him, that is a small grave above a bend in a river. His winnings pay a temple to sweep it. Every autumn he goes there himself, leaves a persimmon on the stone with no name, and talks for a while. She hates being ignored.

Every morning before dawn, wherever he is, he draws the boy’s draw and counts out loud. Matsumaru’s last count was eleven thousand, four hundred and nine. Jūrō picked it up on that riverbank at eleven thousand, four hundred and ten. He is past ninety thousand now, and he has never done it as cleanly as a fourteen-year-old did, once, at midnight, with his sister asleep on his shoulder.

When it’s done, and the blade is home, and the smoke is still rising, he keeps the promise he made with his little finger on a riverbank. He says it quietly, into the smoke, where the castle is still burning and the boy is still inside.
“Good.”
Then, because he was ordered to live: “Again.”

quote: Your name won’t be remembered. Neither will mine.
